name: lecturelens-capture-eval
description: The videos the capture is measured on. Every one of them answers a different question about the capture, and every one of them was checked to see whether the text on the screen can be read at all.

rules.why_height: The size of the text in the picture decides how well it can be read. A video at 360p and one at 1080p differ more than the systems do.
rules.why_one_second: The capture looks at the screen once a second, so the ground truth is built on the same clock.

videos.credit: MIT 6.0001 Introduction to CS and Programming Using Python, Spring 2018, Ana Bell and Eric Grimson

ground_truth.note: The notes are of the same lecture in the term before, and the deck is the same one. The picture of a slide and the page of the notes were matched and the match was between 73 and 88 out of a hundred on the slides that had text on them.

videos.why: The pair of the set. Printed slides that fill the frame and a public text of them, so the reading of the screen is measured against the real thing and not against a reading of it.

ground_truth.note: The slides are a picture of a picture, so the text is read from the picture and checked by hand.

videos.why: Printed slides that fill the frame. The text is read almost without a mistake, so any loss is the fault of the capture and not of the reading.

ground_truth.note: The slides are on a drive of the course. They are the text of the screen once they are fetched.

videos.why: Dense slides with a picture next to them, and a diagram that appears later in the lecture. It is the hard part of the slide case.

videos.license: NPTEL lectures are open for educational use.

ground_truth.note: The lecture is in Hindi and English together, which is the case the notes have to work in.

videos.why: The lectures the user actually records. The language is mixed, so the text and the speech have to be put together.

ground_truth.note: The code is in a repository that is public, so the text on the screen can be found in it.

videos.why: An editor with a picture in it, and the code that is being typed. The text changes line by line, not slide by slide.

ground_truth.note: A browser with the menu bar and the tabs in it. Most of the hundred and fifty lines are not the lecture.

videos.why: The hardest case for the trigger. The window is full of things that are not the lecture, and the reading of the whole frame gives a hundred and fifty lines of which a handful matter.

videos.credit: Papers We Love, Matt Adereth on the January 1965 issue of the CACM

ground_truth.note: The paper is public, so the text on the screen is known.

videos.why: A paper in two columns with figures. The text is small and it is in the middle of the screen.

ground_truth.note: Nothing should be captured. The speech carries the whole lecture.

videos.why: The case the user named. A lecture with no slides must not make the capture work hard, and it must not put the frames of the talking head into the notes.

ground_truth.note: The notes of the course are the text of what was said. The screen has handwriting on a board, so the notes are the speech and not the picture.

videos.why: A board that is written on by hand. The reading of printed text cannot read it, so this one is a case of its own.

not_used.name: MIT 6.006 Fall 2011
not_used.why: The copy on the channel is at 360p and the board is written on by hand. The text cannot be read at that size.

not_used.name: Stanford CS231N slides
not_used.why: The slides of the recent years are on a drive of the course, not on the site. The pictures have to be read by hand.
